the prior question: Before any substantive claim, PMN asks: how do we know? Most frameworks answer implicitly; making it the first analytical move prevents the primary epistemic failure of self-validating systems. (1.1)
primary diagnostic: The most revealing test of any framework: what does it do when its predictions are contradicted by evidence? Does it revise, or insulate itself from correction? (1.2)
probabilistic determinism: Structure shapes what is possible without eliminating the difference that agency makes within those constraints. Apparent contingency conceals identifiable structural forces. (1.3)
insulation: The epistemic failure mode: absorbing contradicting evidence by reinterpreting it rather than revising conclusions. The primary form of intellectual dishonesty this framework tries to prevent. (1.2)
inaction as choice: The analytical recognition that not intervening in an existing arrangement is a material decision that sustains its current dynamics, including its structural production of suffering. (1.5)
truth: A true claim communicated in a way that ensures it will be rejected is not, by practical standards, better than silence. Effective communication of truth is part of its epistemic duty. (1.6)
convergence under material pressure: Different societies facing similar material pressures tend toward similar solutions - not through ideological persuasion but through selection. Also called de facto universalism. (1.4)
de facto universalism: The descriptive observation that similar pressures produce similar institutional solutions across cultures. Driven by material selection, not persuasion. Distinct from normative universalism. (1.4)
productive equilibrium: Belief and doubt held simultaneously - not balanced against each other but maintained in tension. Pure confidence stops testing; pure skepticism cannot distinguish better from worse. (1.6b)
anti-dogmatic principle: Commit fully to the direction while holding specific positions lightly enough that evidence can revise them. The commitment is to the method, not to any particular conclusion. (1.6b)
knowledge production: Who produces knowledge, under what conditions, with what resources, and in whose interest - these material facts shape what questions get asked and which answers get amplified. (1.7)
epistemic infrastructure: The material systems (media, credentialing, archives, distribution networks) through which knowledge is produced, verified, stored, and accessed socially. (1.8-1.12)
epistemic authority: The social capacity to make claims others treat as reliable without independent verification. A structural resource distributed by institutional position, not by accuracy. (1.9)
information asymmetry: The structural gap between what actors inside an arrangement observe and what actors outside or below it can observe. A primary mechanism of institutional power. (1.10)
trust infrastructure: The social relationships and institutional practices that allow actors to extend confidence beyond what they can directly verify. Complex coordination depends on it. (1.11)
trust collapse: Threshold-governed failure of epistemic infrastructure. Once generalized uncertainty is manufactured, social knowledge fragments into incompatible factual communities. (1.11)
epistemic capture: When actors whose material interests are served by particular claims gaining social standing systematically amplify those claims using accumulated epistemic authority. (1.9)
adaptive materialism: The mechanism of change: systems transform through continuous interaction between organisms and conditions - not through guaranteed dialectical contradiction, but through material pressure and selection. (2.2)
adaptive naturalism: The methodology of PMN. Begins from biological foundations. Uses adaptive empirical epistemology. Evaluates all systems against the minimal anchor. Does not prescribe fixed outcomes. (14.1)
reality as primary: Reality exists independently of perception. Different observers converge on the same material limits because those limits exist independently of any observer. (2.1)
interface-emergent phenomena: Properties that appear at higher levels of organization not present in the components. Consciousness and meaning are treated as real without requiring non-material explanation. (5.3)
levels of analysis: Three simultaneous levels - individual, institutional, systemic - that must be kept distinct. Collapsing them produces the most persistent errors in political and social analysis. (7.0b)
biological foundation: The starting point of PMN: organisms that can suffer, and the material consequences of that fact for everything they build. Precedes and grounds culture, production, and institutional history. (3.2)
descriptive egoism: The starting point: self-preservation and avoidance of pain are features of how organisms actually behave - a fact, not a prescription for how they should behave. (3.2)
is-ought bridge: PMN moves from biology to evaluation not via a moral claim but a stability claim: structural suffering produces measurable systemic consequences that can be tracked empirically. (3.3)
minimal anchor: The most defensible universal evaluative criterion: organisms with the capacity to suffer do not choose to suffer. This biological fact grounds evaluation without importing prior moral commitments. (3.4)
structural suffering: Suffering that is imposed (not chosen), preventable (not inherent to the human condition), structurally caused (produced by identifiable institutional arrangements), and disfunctional (serving no developmental purpose for those who bear it). A qualitative classification, not a quantity: the formula S = f(R, B, V) tracks structural tendency, not a measurable sum. The primary variable for system evaluation. (15.0b)
cognitive constraints: Human cognition specific features - limits on genuine social range, systematic bias, in-group preference - that directly constrain which institutional forms are viable. (3.8)
cooperative substrate: The foundation of trust, reciprocity, and long-term investment that complex social organization requires. Structural suffering degrades it; arrangements that minimize suffering maintain it. (2.2)
causal chain: Collectively organized societies emerge from self-interested organisms through identifiable intermediate steps - coordination solutions to problems self-interest alone cannot solve. (3.7)
stability claim: The is-ought bridge: arrangements that produce unnecessary suffering generate systemic instability. An empirical observation about material consequences, not a prior moral axiom. (3.3)
evaluative criterion: Does this arrangement produce more or less unnecessary structural suffering than available alternatives? Comparative, contextual, and falsifiable. (4.2)
progress: Stripped of teleological content: not history moving toward a predetermined end, but arrangements that produce less unnecessary suffering than their predecessors. (4.3)
genuine development: Beyond the minimal anchor: not merely the absence of pain, but the expansion of what becomes possible for organisms when the biological floor is secured. (2.2)
consistency standard: Standards applied to some actors and not others are preferences dressed as principles. The same lens must be applied to actors one is sympathetic to as to those one is critical of. (8.3)
manipulation: The recognition that stated motivations and material interests diverge systematically requires structural checks - and can be used for emancipatory or controlling purposes alike. (4.4)
power as structural position: Power is not primarily a property of individuals but of structural positions. Structural incentives shape behavior regardless of the intentions of whoever occupies the position. (6.2)
power asymmetry: The condition in which different actors within a system have significantly different capacities to shape outcomes, define terms, and determine whose suffering is visible. (6.3)
institutional capture: The process by which an institution designed to regulate or limit power is subordinated to the interests of the power it was designed to regulate, while maintaining its formal appearance of independence. (7.3b)
legitimacy: The social recognition that an arrangement has the right to function as it does. A functional condition arrangements require to operate without continuous coercion - not a moral judgment. (10.13)
performance legitimacy: Legitimacy derived from delivering outcomes subjects experience as beneficial. The most fragile form: requires continuous delivery and is immediately undermined by visible failure. (6.7)
procedural legitimacy: Legitimacy derived from following recognized rules and processes, independent of outcomes. More durable than performance legitimacy but vulnerable to capture. (6.7)
narrative legitimacy: Legitimacy derived from compelling accounts of why the arrangement deserves to exist. Can persist long after performance and procedural legitimacy have eroded. (6.7)
legitimacy deficit: Accumulated damage to social recognition of an arrangement right to function. Threshold-governed: once exceeded, the arrangement loses the consent it needs to operate. (15.7)
self-preservation mechanisms: How institutions develop behaviors that protect their continuation independently of their ostensible purpose - following from the material interests of those who operate them. (6.5)
the state problem: The state reflects particular distributions of power, not a neutral arbiter. The challenge is to use it as an instrument for reducing structural suffering while accounting for this structural bias. (7.1)
progressive institutionalism: Institutions are necessary coordination mechanisms required indefinitely. They require constant scrutiny, genuine accountability, and structural capacity for substantive reform. (7.2)
substantive reform: Procedural reform changes rules. Substantive reform changes who controls resources and what outcomes the system actually produces. The distinction identifies whether change is real. (7.2)
custodian problem: Every arrangement designed to hold power accountable generates the same problem at a higher level: who watches the watchers? Structural, not solvable by finding better people. (7.3)
noble lie: Fictions governing arrangements maintain about themselves that do not correspond to what they actually produce. Named from Plato; analyzed as a structural phenomenon, not a conspiratorial one. (7.5)
path dependence: The costs of switching from existing institutional arrangements mean initial choices persist long after the conditions that produced them have changed. History constrains the present materially. (7.7)
system: A complex adaptive arrangement of organisms, institutions, resource flows, and incentive structures that interact across multiple levels simultaneously. (15.1)
intersectional analysis: Structural exclusions operate through multiple intersecting axes. Acknowledging this is necessary but not sufficient; the procedure must specify which axis is most explanatory in a given context. (8.2b)
governing narrative: The dominant story a society tells about itself that shapes which outcomes are treated as legitimate, which causes are visible, and which forms of suffering are counted. (8.4)
meritocracy as visibility suppression: The meritocratic narrative recategorizes structural causation as individual causation - misreading outcomes produced by institutional position as outcomes produced by individual capacity. (8.4c)
anti-naive universalism: Universal standards can be genuine without being neutral. Applying them requires accounting for asymmetric starting conditions produced by historical processes. (8.5)
material geography: The distribution of natural resources, arable land, and strategic geography that shapes what is possible in international relations beneath ideology and institutional design. (9.0)
historical divergence: The divergence between territories with capacity for self-determination and those without was produced by colonialism and extraction - not by geography or cultural difference alone. (9.0b)
parallel development framework: Materially different societies require different institutional paths toward similar outcomes - rejecting both imposition of one model and pure relativism. (9.4)
structural realism: States pursue power and security; norms are routinely violated when they conflict with state interest; the gap between declared values and actual behavior is permanent. (9.1)
geopolitical power concentration: Concentration of power in a single dominant actor produces systematically dangerous conditions regardless of the ideological commitments of the concentrating actor. (9.3b)
transformation pressure: T = A = S x D x P x G - the net force pushing a system toward significant reorganisation, identical to accumulated pressure (15.4). Repressive capacity does not subtract from T: it modifies the threshold T must cross to produce non-linear reorganisation. The full trajectory formula integrates these as Tr = T / (C x L) - CP (15.9). When T exceeds the system's threshold - itself variable and not knowable in advance - rapid reorganisation becomes probable. (15.2)
threshold non-linearity: Systems absorb incremental pressure up to a threshold, beyond which they reorganize rapidly and unpredictably. Pre-threshold behavior does not predict post-threshold behavior. (10.5)
windows of political opportunity: Moments when the cost of fundamental change falls and the cost of maintaining the status quo rises simultaneously. Produced by structural conditions, not created by actors. See also: political window (Tw). (10.5b)
counter-power: Organized capacity of populations to constrain institutional behavior - the mechanism through which transformation pressure becomes political force. (10.9)
reform vs revolution: Substantially a debate about sequencing and threshold management. Reform is appropriate when the system retains sufficient legitimacy; revolutionary change becomes relevant at threshold conditions. (10.6)
two modes of struggle: Hero: actors operating through publicly legitimate channels. Vigilante: actors operating outside those channels. Both carry specific structural risks regardless of their justification. (10.10)
resource deprivation (R): The gap between what a population requires to meet the minimal anchor - the biological floor - and what the arrangement actually provides. Not absolute poverty: R is always relative to what the arrangement could provide and has committed to provide, explicitly or implicitly. It is zero when the floor is met, and non-zero when the arrangement produces floor deprivation that is structurally caused and preventable. (15.0b)
institutional betrayal (B): The gap between the function an institution claims to perform and what it actually produces for the populations it claims to serve. An institution that has never promised anything cannot betray: it is the promise - explicit or implicit in the mandate, the legal obligation, or the legitimating narrative - that creates the betrayal when systematically broken. Not corruption or bad intent, but the structural outcome of capture dynamics that redirect institutional function without eliminating institutional claim-making. Because B presupposes a prior normative contract, exclusion never covered by such a promise is a separate variable (E). (15.0b)
stress-testing: Applying extreme cases and taboo questions to test the logical consistency of a position. A position that cannot survive its extreme implications requires revision. (12.1)
multi-perspectival analysis: Analyzing the same situation through multiple theoretical lenses - not to relativize conclusions, but to identify what each lens sees that the others miss. (12.2)
genealogical interrogation: Asking of any institution, belief, or norm: how did this come to exist? Whose interests did it serve at origin? What material conditions maintain it now? (12.6)
framework failure: Scope creep, stability bias, observer position effects, coordination neglect, and treating permanent tensions as solvable contradictions. Knowing these is required for honest application. (12.5)
tensions: Contradictions are structural incompatibilities requiring transformation. Tensions are genuine conflicts of real values that must be managed, not resolved. Misclassifying either produces serious errors. (13.1b)
progressive materialist naturalism: The doctrine: the current application of Adaptive Naturalism to existing material conditions. Temporal, conditional, and expected to change as conditions change. (14.2)
permanent conditions: Features of human social organization that persist across historical periods: resource scarcity, cognitive constraints, cooperative substrate requirements, power dynamics, and structural suffering. (11.2)
primary formula: The master relationship all predictive analysis in the framework reduces to: T = A = S x D x P x G, with the shorthand T = S x D x P omitting G for legibility though G is always implied. Each variable is itself produced by a secondary formula, so the primary formula is the output and the rest are the inputs. Note the symbols: A is accumulated pressure, not adaptive capacity, which is C. (15.2)
social ontological emergence: Social structures have genuine causal properties that cannot be fully reduced to the properties of their individual components. The pattern of systemic outcomes produced by institutional arrangements cannot be derived from individual psychology or biology alone. (2.4)
layered constraint model: The ontological architecture of PMN: physical/biological conditions constrain what economic configurations are viable; economic configurations constrain what political arrangements are stable; each layer has genuine causal properties not fully determined by the layer below. (2.2)
reductionism: The analytical error of explaining persistent structural outcomes by reference to aggregated individual choices, treating actors as operating in a structurally neutral environment. Misses the causal role of the institutional structure within which choices are made. (2.5)
idealism: The analytical error of treating ideas, culture, or discourse as the primary determinants of social outcomes, treating material conditions as derivative of ideational structures. The mirror error to reductionism. (2.5)
dispositional harm prevention: The institutional design problem of engaging with individuals who carry a risk of harming others before harm is acted upon. Enforcement-only institutions cannot solve this class of problem; preventive pathways are required. (3.4c)
agent ecology: The distributed ecosystem of actors — operating inside and outside institutions — whose independent actions, shared analysis, and performed hostilities produce complementary structural effects without centralized coordination. (10.10c)
hero-vigilante: The two-mode model of strategic action: actors who operate within institutional constraints (heroes) and actors who operate outside them (vigilantes), whose functional interdependence is concealed by necessary surface hostility. (10.10c)
performative hostility: The strategic appearance of conflict between insider and outsider actors that protects both — insiders preserve institutional access, outsiders preserve credibility — while genuine coordination continues beneath the surface. (10.10b)
asymmetric defection: The failure mode in which insider actors distance themselves from outside pressure in ways that go beyond performance: actively delegitimizing outside actors, converting performed hostility into actual opposition. (10.10b)
institutional drift: The structural process by which actors who begin as genuine reformers are gradually captured by the incentives of their position, each small compromise appearing justified until they operate entirely within the logic of the system they were opposing. (10.12)
distributed accountability: The ecosystem's mechanism for evaluating whether actors are still performing their function: judgment arising from multiple independent perspectives, based on behavioral evidence, with thresholds set by material outcomes rather than personal loyalty. (10.14)
self-neutralization: The rarest form of strategic discipline: an actor recognizing they have become compromised or counterproductive and withdrawing before the ecosystem must do so from outside. Places the objective above identity. (10.13)
meaning problem of abundance: The tension that arises when material constraints historically necessary for genuine becoming are progressively eliminated: if cognitive effort, relational friction, and creative resistance are removed, becoming may cease to take meaningful form. (13.4b)
subject boundary problem: The tension at the technological horizon where PMN's evaluative criterion — developed for human subjects with specific biological capacities — cannot straightforwardly evaluate transformations that would produce subjects of a fundamentally different kind. (3.4d)
variation-deficit conflation: The analytical error of treating biological or psychological variation as deficiency, when the suffering associated with the variation is produced by institutional design treating it as a deviation from a standard the variation does not violate. (13.4e)
accommodation: Two institutional strategies for variation: accommodation adds provisions within an existing baseline; transformation contests the baseline itself, designing for the full range of human variation from the start. (13.4f)
internalized norms: Behavioral and affective patterns installed through social practice before they are available for rational examination. Structurally produced but not thereby beyond the possibility of re-practice and gradual reorganization. (13.4g)
moral-functional tension: The tension between the moral critique of an institution and its functional analysis: institutions perform coordination, meaning-transmission, and social reproduction functions that persist even when their stated purposes or moral claims are discredited. (13.4h)
technology as constraint-modifier: Technologies whose primary effect is to change the constraint structure within which institutional and individual choice operates, rather than merely expanding options within an unchanged structure. The framework's analytical category for major technologies. (16.0)
technological leverage point: A position in the institutional architecture — created during technological transitions — from which disproportionate influence over the outcomes of many actors can be exercised. Capture of leverage points is the primary mechanism of technological inequality. (16.1)
capture timing: The structural dynamic by which leverage points are captured during the transition period, before populations have organized to contest them, allowing capturing actors to shape the institutional framework before effective opposition forms. (16.1)
AI as institutional architecture: AI's primary effect is on the institutional layer itself: modifying what organizational configurations are viable, changing information processing and decision-making capacities, and systematically reconfiguring accountability relationships. (16.2)
algorithmic governance: Decision-making by systems whose criteria are not interpretable by those affected, producing a qualitative change in accountability architecture: affected individuals cannot contest decisions whose basis they cannot examine. (1.11)
biological floor: The differential availability of biotechnological capabilities across institutional contexts. When the same biological conditions are survivable in some contexts and fatal in others due to institutional arrangements, the floor is an institutional determination, not a natural given. (3.1)
acceleration problem: The dynamic in which technologies that accelerate subsequent development — particularly AI — produce rates of institutional change that systematically outpace social capacity for meaning infrastructure adaptation. (16.4)
becoming: The capacity to develop cognitively, morally, and creatively beyond the conditions determined by birth. The ceiling of PMN's evaluative framework. A life worth living has a trajectory of becoming, not merely survival or consumption. Borrowed from Aristotle (eudaimonia) and Nietzsche, but democratized: structurally accessible to all, not reserved for a genius elite. (4.5)
visibility suppression: The degree to which suffering is prevented from becoming collectively legible - through information control, narrative management that attributes structural conditions to individual failure, isolation of those who suffer, or algorithmic architecture that suppresses structurally relevant claims. V is not an additive component of suffering: it is the conversion variable determining how much of the suffering produced by R and B translates into organised transformation pressure. (15.0b)
meaning infrastructure: The network of institutions, narratives, rituals, and daily practices that orient collective life, answer 'what is worth living for', and make long-term sacrifice legible. When meaning infrastructure collapses (disenchantment), the vacancy is not filled by pure rationality but by the most available ideology — historically, the most violent ones. (5.6)
elite circulation: The process by which individuals in power are replaced while the power structure itself remains intact. New faces with fresh promises occupy the same positions with the same rules and the same incentives. The mechanism by which systems absorb revolutionary pressure without fundamental transformation. (Pareto, Mosca.). (6.8)
adaptive capacity (C): The ability of a system to absorb pressure and demands for change without altering its fundamental structure. The higher the adaptive capacity, the harder the system is to force into transformation. Formula: C = (F × E × I) × (1 − K). The 'immune system' of a regime. (15.5)
repressive capacity (Rc): The ability of a system to use coercion and violence to maintain itself. Formula: Rc = (Cv × El × Ic) × (1 − Io). The final instrument when legitimacy is exhausted and adaptive capacity has failed. Critically dependent on the loyalty of the enforcers — the most fragile variable in the formula. (15.6)
fracture lines: Divisions within a population that prevent unified action against a common structural cause. May be material (genuinely divergent interests) or manufactured (amplified by power to divide). Distinguishing which type is the most strategically crucial analytical task for counter-power building. (10.9)
the watcher problem: The danger in movement ecosystems of hidden actors — internal or external — who quietly coordinate or manipulate multiple factions toward ends unknown to the participants. The modern form of the agent-provocateur problem, now operating through funding flows and information architecture rather than physical infiltration. (10.10c-ii)
rent-seeking: The behavior of actors who extract value not by creating new value but by manipulating the social, political, or legal environment to capture existing value. The signature of advanced capitalist decay: when genuine innovation becomes harder than regulatory capture, capital shifts to lobbying, acquisition of competitors, and monopoly entrenchment. (7.3c)
narrative infrastructure: The specific layer of meaning infrastructure consisting of the large stories that organize collective perception of past (history), present (identity), and future (hope). The 'operating system' of collective consciousness. In the media-algorithm era, narrative infrastructure is contested across multiple simultaneous competing narratives rather than one dominant story. (8.4)
the seeker: The actor type produced by meaning infrastructure collapse: intelligent, critical, capable of deconstructing all ideology and illusion, but unable to build new frameworks. Trapped in permanent critique without action. An asset if managed, a liability if allowed to lead. The Nietzschean diagnosis of the modern critical intellectual. (4.5)
ecological constraint: The absolute outer limit imposed by planetary finitude on all human systems. Not an environmental add-on but a condition of possibility: ecological destruction forecloses the biological foundation on which becoming depends. The framework's hardest criticism of classical materialism's assumption of unlimited growth. (3.10)
surpassability: The framework's highest commitment to its own obsolescence. A successful analytical framework is one that generates its successor — makes itself unnecessary by producing better frameworks. The most radical anti-dogmatic principle: fidelity to the framework is less important than fidelity to the questions it was built to answer. (14.4)
visibility variable: The V slot in the structural suffering formula. Its direction follows the name: V measures suppression, so a high V means structural harm is largely prevented from becoming collectively legible, not that it is well documented. Meritocracy narrative and algorithmic curation are the primary contemporary mechanisms (8.4c); the canonical definition is at 15.0b.
cosmological capture: A failure mode where actors operating within a deeply naturalized belief system cannot perceive their own capture, experiencing systemic constraints as laws of nature or divine necessity rather than as alterable arrangements. (7.3c)
coalition width (W): The breadth of the counter-power coalition measured by the range of structurally distinct groups whose material interests converge in opposing a given arrangement. W is not headcount but structural diversity: a coalition of ten organisations from identical structural positions scores lower W than a coalition of three organisations from positions with different material stakes and different channels of institutional access. High W increases the counter-power formula (15.8) because structurally diverse coalitions are harder to fragment through targeted concession and can apply pressure across multiple institutional leverage points simultaneously. W degrades when coalitions narrow to identity-homogeneous membership or when tactical success concentrates organisational resources in one faction. (15.0b)
institutional fragmentation (If): The degree to which the institutions sustaining a dominant arrangement are internally divided in interest, authority, or enforcement capacity. If is a structural variable of the target system, not of the counter-power coalition. High If indicates that elite cohesion has broken down: factions within the governing arrangement are competing for position in ways that create openings for counter-power that a unified elite would close. If interacts with W in the counter-power formula (15.8): high If creates structural opportunity, but high W is required to exploit it organisationally. If is one of the primary mechanisms through which transformation windows (10.5b) open: elite fragmentation typically precedes threshold crossing in historical cases where transformation pressure alone was insufficient to produce transition. (15.0b)
absolute structural exclusion (E): Structural suffering produced by arrangements that deny ontological standing to a group from inception, without ever having extended a normative promise of inclusion that could subsequently be violated. E is analytically distinct from B (Institutional Betrayal): B requires a prior normative contract whose breach generates the political charge; E operates where no such contract was ever offered. Caste systems, chattel slavery, and apartheid are paradigmatic E configurations — they do not betray; they exclude by constitutive design. This distinction matters for the formula architecture because E-produced suffering does not generate the same transformation pressure dynamics as B-produced suffering: populations subject to E have no legitimacy claim to invoke against the arrangement, which systematically forecloses the institutional channels through which B-generated pressure can accumulate. Counter-power under E conditions requires constructing the standing that B conditions assume as pre-existing. See 3.4 (Ambedkar note) and Intellectual Debts. (15.0b)
layer / level: Layer refers to the constraint model verticality: Ecological Viability → Biological Floor → Economic Arrangements → Institutional Architecture → Meaning Infrastructure (2.2). Each layer operates as a precondition for those above it. Level refers to the scale of analysis: micro (individual/household), meso (organisation/community), macro (system/state). These are orthogonal dimensions. A meso-level analysis can examine the biological layer; a macro-level analysis can examine the meaning infrastructure layer. Conflating layer and level produces analytic confusion about whether a claim is about causal priority (layer) or analytical scope (level). (15.0b)
structural tendency analysis: The PMN methodology that predicts systemic trajectories and threshold proximities rather than specific events, forms, or actors. It operates by applying complex systems dynamics (f_Cs) to the dynamic interaction (⊕) of natural sciences (Ns), human sciences (Hs), and historical dynamics (Hd). Formula: STA = f_Cs(Ns ⊕ Hs ⊕ Hd). (15.9)
generating conditions: The set of structural factors whose presence is necessary and sufficient to produce a given outcome. In PMN diagnostic analysis, identifying generating conditions explains why a phenomenon exists rather than merely describing it. Contrasted with eliminating conditions. (XIII). (13.1c)
elimination conditions: The set of changes to structure that, if achieved, would end or substantially reduce a harmful outcome. Distinct from generating conditions: a system can be understood without knowing how to dismantle it. PMN requires both to be named. (XIII). (13.1c)
diagnostic boundary: The threshold between what a framework can reliably analyze and what lies outside its current explanatory range. PMN treats its own diagnostic boundary as a live question, not a fixed limit. (XIII). (13.4)
preferential access (capture stage 1): Preferential access: the first stage of institutional capture, where specific actors gain disproportionate access to decision-makers without yet altering stated criteria or formal rules. (VII, XIV). (7.3b)
preference alignment (capture stage 2): Preference alignment: the second stage of institutional capture, where the institution begins adjusting its informal priorities to match those of the capturing actor, while formal rules remain unchanged. (VII, XIV). (7.3b)
criteria redefinition (capture stage 3): Criteria redefinition: the third stage of institutional capture, where the formal evaluative criteria are rewritten to structurally favor the capturing actor, making the advantage appear merit-based. (VII, XIV). (7.3b)
completed capture (capture stage 4): Completed capture: the final stage of institutional capture, where the institution operates as an instrument of the capturing actor's interests while maintaining the appearance of independence and legitimacy. (VII, XIV). (7.3b)
chosen versus imposed: A key distinction in PMN's suffering typology. Chosen suffering is voluntarily accepted in pursuit of a goal; imposed suffering is structurally produced without the subject's meaningful consent. PMN focuses diagnostic attention on the latter. (III). (3.4b)
functional versus disfunctional: Functional suffering produces learning, adaptation, or resistance; disfunctional suffering produces only harm with no compensating structural effect. PMN does not treat suffering as inherently meaningful but does recognize this distinction for strategic analysis. (III). (3.4b)
structural versus incidental: Structural suffering is produced systematically by institutional arrangements and is therefore predictable and addressable at the institutional level. Incidental suffering arises from contingent individual events. PMN's primary domain is the former. (III). (3.4b)
material versus existential: Material suffering involves deprivation of physical, economic, or social goods (food, safety, shelter, participation). Existential suffering involves loss of meaning, purpose, or ontological stability. PMN analyzes both but treats material suffering as the prior diagnostic layer. (III). (3.4b)
the foundation of value: The evaluative standard of the framework, derived from the biological foundation rather than from any cultural tradition, historical stage, or system of production. It answers the question Marx declined to answer directly - why the suffering a system produces is bad - without critiquing a system by standards that system itself generated. (4.1)
better and worse: The comparative criterion above the floor. The minimal anchor sets a threshold but does not rank arrangements that both clear it. Better arrangements preserve and expand adaptive response capacity across the population and reduce the conditions that foreclose it, by means that do not restore floor-level violations in other populations or in future generations. The criterion is directional, not binary; distributional, not aggregate. (4.2)
horizon and instrument: The distinction economic doctrine requires. The horizon is the direction the minimal anchor points toward; the instrument is the arrangement most materially effective at moving toward it under current conditions. A horizon keeps development from becoming circular without requiring that it be reached in any specific form or timeline. Confusing the two converts a reference point into a blueprint. (11.3)
meaning as material condition: The treatment of meaning infrastructure - shared narrative, ritual, community, interpretive framework - as a material variable rather than an epiphenomenon of economic arrangements or a private psychological matter. It is the system through which populations make sense of suffering, organise obligation, and orient collective action, which places it inside the constraint structure rather than above it. (5.6)
the anti-technocratic guardrail: The structural refusal to treat superior analysis as a warrant for governing. Technocratic governance - concentrating decision authority in those who claim superior analytical capacity - is not the implication of this analysis but the capture of it by the actors already best positioned to claim it. (6.4)
scale as a structural variable: The treatment of scale as a variable with predictable effects on the custodian problem, the capture sequence, and the distribution of becoming conditions - rather than as a fixed trade-off between coordination capacity and accountability. The trade-off is real but not given: institutional design and the material conditions of information, coordination, and counter-power modify what it is at each level. (7.0c)
the material basis of international orde: The geography of water, energy, arable land, and strategic position that determines which choices states can make and at what cost. Not background context for the analysis of power but the constraint structure within which the rest of the analysis operates. A transformation programme that ignores it produces recommendations coherent in the abstract and impossible in the specific configuration where they must be applied. (9.0)
the organizational form problem: The question of what structural properties the container of counter-power must have. It is prior to the accumulation mechanisms, because capacity built inside an organisational form is deployed or redirected according to that form's properties. The tradition analysis yields a consistent negative finding: every major form counter-power movements have adopted fails the custodian problem in characteristic ways. (10.8)
technocratic drift constraints: Structural requirements on applying PMN in institutional settings, imposed because the framework's complexity advantages actors with more time, education, and institutional access - whose fluency becomes interpretive authority that others cannot easily contest. The safeguard does not reduce complexity, which would remove analytical power; it forces accessibility and distributed verification independent of individual capacity. The framework applying 6.4 to itself. (12.8)
domain-specific formulas: Refinements of the primary formula for domains where the relevant variables take specific forms, such as geopolitical power shift. They do not replace the primary formula; they specify how its variables are instantiated within a domain. (15.10)
the arc from physiology to institution: The sequence by which institutions emerge from biological starting points, consistent enough across independent civilisations to be treated as structural rather than contingent: organisms avoid pain and seek resources; scarcity turns that into conflict; coordination outperforms unrestrained competition in most circumstances; stable coordination mechanisms become institutions; institutions require enforcement, which generates authority. Authority is materially legitimate while it solves the coordination problems that produced it. (3.6)
the capture sequence: The recognisable stages through which institutional capture proceeds, distinct from the conditions that make it probable. The custodian problem (7.3) identifies when capture becomes likely; the sequence specifies how it advances - access asymmetry, then the shift of the decision filter, then criteria redefinition, then completed capture. The early stages present as specialisation and efficiency, which is why capture is rarely visible while it is still reversible. (7.3c-i)
power beyond ownership: The mechanisms through which concentrated power produces capture and structural suffering with significant independence from ownership: expertise monopoly, information asymmetry, and network effects. The economic doctrine is organised around ownership because of its demonstrated relationship to capture (7.3c); this names where that organisation is incomplete. An account that tracks only ownership will miss concentration that has migrated to these three. (11.5)
thresholds and non-linearity: The property of complex adaptive systems by which incremental pressure is absorbed up to a point, beyond which the system reorganises rapidly and in ways not predictable from its pre-threshold behaviour. It makes incrementalism - small changes, observe, adjust - potentially catastrophic near a threshold, because the observed response stops being a guide to the next one. The pattern recurs across ecological limits, institutional legitimacy, and social cohesion. (10.5)
who watches the watchers: The accountability problem applied to the counter-power ecosystem itself: who judges when a movement or its leadership has become what it organised against. Centralised hierarchy answers this at costs documented across the twentieth century. The answer here is distributed judgement from genuinely independent perspectives, resting on behavioural evidence rather than personal loyalty, with thresholds set by what is produced materially rather than by who claims most loudly to know. (10.14)
conflicting genuine suffering claims: Cases in which two or more parties each hold genuine, floor-level suffering claims that no single institutional configuration can fully honour. Distinct from competing preferences, interests, or goods: the claims meet the threshold for analytical consideration, honouring one fully requires conditions that sustain the other, and they are not dissolved by procedural neutrality. (13.2c)
formula limits: The acknowledged limits of the formulas, stated as part of the theory rather than as a caveat appended to protect it. They predict structural tendency and threshold proximity, not the specific form, timing, or actors of transformation; whether accumulated pressure resolves as reform, revolution, collapse, or repressive consolidation depends on contingencies the structural formula does not determine. They also cannot assign precise coefficients. (15.13)
education as structural variable: Education treated as a domain with its own capture dynamics and failure modes, not merely as an instrument of other variables. Its structural position is peculiar because it operates on both levels of the evaluative architecture at once: it is where visibility suppression is maintained or reduced, and where becoming is expanded or foreclosed across generations. (8.7)
multipolarity as transitional arrangemen: The distribution of effective power across multiple actors with differing interests, preferable to unipolarity under current conditions for the same material reasons distributed institutional design is preferable to concentrated design: lower systemic capture risk, lower cost of mistakes, and preserved competition that makes institutional accountability possible. Transitional, not terminal - the long-term aim is coordination at global scale, not permanent state competition. (9.3)
ecological debt: The correction that parallel development requires. Building from one's own material starting point is analytically sound, but starting points are not distributed by natural conditions alone: they are products of historical processes, colonial extraction among them. Treating the distribution as given naturalises an arrangement that extraction produced. (9.5)
regime types: The application of the evaluative criterion to regime types that have actually existed, without prior commitment to any institutional form. Diagnostic rather than polemical: each type is assessed for what it gets right as well as wrong, and under which material conditions it has produced better or worse outcomes by the framework's standard. The commitment is to the criterion, not to any regime that happens to satisfy it under some conditions. (7.8)
the starting point: Where the framework begins: not with a claim about what people ought to value, but with a biological observation - organisms avoid pain and approach conditions that support their functioning. This is not a normative premise that someone with different values can contest; it is a structural fact about the organisms that build institutions, and it constrains which arrangements will work. Normative premises can be disputed indefinitely, which is what makes frameworks built on them useless in practice. (3.2)
social ontology: The extension of the materialist ontology to the social level: institutions, cultural frameworks, legal systems, and economic arrangements have genuine causal properties that cannot be fully reduced to the psychology and biology of the individuals who compose them. The defence matters because reductionism is not merely intellectually tempting - it is politically convenient for those whose interests are served by treating social arrangements as natural rather than constructed. (2.4)
those who stand on others: Actors whose material position depends on arrangements that produce structural suffering for others. The observation is structural, not moral: it concerns incentives produced by position, not the character of those occupying it. People whose wealth, status, and security are produced by arrangements that constrain others' development have rational reasons to maintain them - not from intended harm, but because the alternative carries a material cost their position has not prepared them to absorb. Naive analyses of power miss this by looking for malice. (7.6)
political time: The specific quality of a moment that makes it more or less available for particular kinds of action. Thresholds (10.5) describe when a system becomes structurally available for change; political time answers why change occurs in one moment and not in another that is structurally equivalent. Two situations can share threshold proximity, stress distribution, and actor configuration while one transforms and the other stabilises - and the difference is not noise. (10.5b)
drift mechanisms: How actors change position without changing intention. No position in the ecosystem is permanent: the structural incentives of a position gradually shift what an actor considers possible, acceptable, and threatening, through an accumulation of small compromises each of which appears justified by conditions - until the actor operates entirely within the logic of the system they set out to oppose. The process is not dramatic, which is why it is rarely detected while it is still reversible. (10.12)
narrative typology: The classification of governing narratives by the temporal orientation they embed. Governing narratives are material forces (8.4): they shape what populations perceive as possible, which coalitions can form, and which arrangements retain legitimacy. They also structure how populations relate to time - determining the horizon across which collective action can be sustained, the direction from which legitimacy is claimed, and the emotional register through which transformation pressure is experienced. Two societies facing identical material conditions may respond differently because of it. (8.4b)
the strategic equilibrium problem: The framework's tensions in their most acute form: what it actually recommends when the trajectory of transformative technology runs against the demonstrated fragility of meaning infrastructure. The answer begins by refusing the framing - the apparent choice between the two available positions is false, and accepting it on the terms in which it is usually put produces worse outcomes than recognising what it conceals. (13.4d)
the variation-deficit tension: The question of when an institutional response treats human variation as a deficiency requiring correction and when as a characteristic requiring accommodation. Populations vary across cognitive profile, sensory processing, emotional regulation, physical capacity, and communication mode; some of that variation is produced by identifiable developmental conditions, much of it is the natural range of a species with significant plasticity. The tension is permanent because the answer cannot be given once for all variation types. (13.4e)
the suffering variable: The formula for what feeds transformation pressure: S = R + B + V, with V operating as a political-conversion modifier rather than an additive component. It captures the political-dynamic dimension of suffering, not its total quantity. Resource deprivation generates pressure not when hardship is severe but when it is understood as structural, differential, and produced by identifiable arrangements - populations can sustain extraordinary hardship without generating pressure when the deprivation is read as natural, shared, or temporary. (15.3)
the compressed core: The framework stated without its architecture: not a summary, which would require having read the document, but a minimum viable version requiring only three ideas. The full architecture - seventeen parts, a formula system, hundreds of diagnostic questions - is needed for the most demanding analytical work, but the architecture is not the framework. Users who master the three ideas can apply the orientation without the full system; users who study the whole document should be able to derive them independently. (15.15)
the evaluative standard for metaphysical: How metaphysical claims are assessed: by identifying where they make contact with material reality - where they predict or explain something that can in principle be examined. A claim producing no observable consequences cannot be assigned explanatory weight; it can be left open. A claim that does make contact is examined by the standards applying to any empirical claim: consistency, predictability, falsifiability, and responsiveness to counter-evidence. What follows from a successful examination is more limited than metaphysical traditions usually claim. (5.4)
the loop model: How becoming emerges, stated as an observable pattern rather than a destination. The conditions that produce suffering - deprivation, damage, vulnerability, dependency, limitation - trigger responses; responses reduce some suffering while generating new configurations of constraint; successful patterns get encoded in habit, institutional procedure, cultural knowledge, and built infrastructure; encoding lowers the cost of future responses while creating new vulnerabilities and dependencies. Becoming is not teleological. (4.5b)
incentive architecture: The structural features of institutional design that make certain failure modes predictable regardless of the intentions of the actors occupying institutional positions. The custodian problem describes what happens when an institution is targeted by capture from outside; incentive architecture describes what happens when it fails from inside, through the normal functioning of its own incentive structure. (7.3c)
anti-capture design: The institutional structures that have historically reduced the rate and extent of capture, and the design principles derivable from that record. The custodian problem (7.3) cannot be solved, only managed. No design is universally effective: context determines which mechanisms are available and which will be subverted, and the history of anti-capture institutions is also a history of their eventual capture. (7.3d)
religion as material variable: The treatment of religion as a material variable for institutional design, policy analysis, and political strategy, regardless of one's metaphysical commitments. The materialist tradition reached this insight and then misapplied it - recognising that religion has material consequences while treating those consequences as the product of an error correctable by replacing belief with more accurate belief. The correction did not work: belief systems proved more durable than the theory predicted, and attempts to accelerate their dissolution produced results materially worse than tolerating them. (5.5)
anti-passive multiculturalism: The rejection of the position that all cultural practices deserve equal respect and that criticism of any practice is cultural imperialism - made not from hostility to diversity, which the framework values, but from applying the same consistency standard used everywhere else. That standard requires evaluating every cultural practice by the same criterion, including those of dominant cultures and those presenting themselves as universal civilisation rather than as particular culture. (8.6)
realism and direction: The permanent tension between two positions on international relations that the framework holds at once: that the system currently operates broadly as structural realism describes - states pursue power and security, norms yield to interest, and the gap between declared values and actual behaviour is a standing feature - and that the long-term trajectory should move toward stronger cooperation and arrangements more directly accountable to human welfare across existing boundaries. Neither position cancels the other. (9.1)
technology as redistributor of material: Technology as a structural force that reshapes the terrain on which political actors operate, rather than a tool those actors deploy. It changes who holds power, and does so in ways not controlled by the arrangements that existed before it appeared - one of the most reliable patterns in the historical record and among the most systematically underestimated. The printing press did not merely make books cheaper; it broke the institutional monopoly on the production and distribution of authorised knowledge. (9.2b)
the is-ought bridge: How the framework crosses from description to evaluation without asserting that suffering is morally bad. Hume's objection is treated as formally correct: no quantity of facts closes the gap. The move is to dissolve the problem rather than leap it - the step from biology to evaluation is not a moral claim but a stability claim. Suffering that is structural, systematic, and without compensating function has consequences for the arrangement producing it, and those consequences are observable. (3.3)
suffering comparison: The procedure for comparing forms of structural suffering when they conflict. The typology (3.4b) distinguishes forms without providing a way to weigh them against each other, and trade-off conditions - where reducing one form necessarily increases another, or the same resources cannot address several at once - are not exceptional but the normal condition of any arrangement operating under constraint. A framework that can classify suffering but not compare it has classified a problem without supplying the means to act on the classification. (3.4e)
non-human sentients: The minimal doctrinal position on sentient beings outside the human case, stated first by what it forbids: it licenses no utilitarian aggregation across entity categories. Units of non-human suffering cannot be summed against units of human becoming with the larger sum winning - 3.4c establishes that aggregation as a category error, a misapplication of the framework as a pain-calculator rather than as a structural analysis of the conditions for becoming. The prohibition is the prerequisite for the position, not a caveat on it. (3.4c-ii)
relational ontology: The claim, reached independently across several traditions, that the unit of social reality is not the isolated individual organism but the person constituted through relation - Ubuntu's umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, the Confucian ren as benevolence constituted through social roles rather than preceding them, Aristotle's zoon politikon fulfilled only within the polis. It operates at a different level of analysis from the descriptive egoism of the starting point (3.2), not in contradiction to it. (3.2b)
affective mobilization: The emotional states that motivate political behaviour directly, often independently of and sometimes against material interest calculation. Fear, humiliation, status anxiety, and collective grief are not irrational distortions of judgement that dissolve once material conditions are explained clearly; they are evolved responses to specific categories of condition. Distinct from cognitive constraints (3.8), which limit rational information processing rather than supplying motivation. (3.8b)
stable irrationality: Patterns of behaviour that are irrational by the standard of the actor's own material interests, persist across time and generations, cannot be reduced to information deficits or affective capture, and are reproduced by social structures in ways that make them effectively stable features of the system. Analytically distinct from cognitive constraint and affective mobilisation, both of which treat irrationality as a limitation on rational response rather than as something structurally reproduced. (3.8c)
demographic dynamics: Population structure treated as a material variable rather than as background: age distribution, growth rate, urban-rural distribution, geographic density. These change, and when they do, systems built around the previous distribution face structural pressures that ideology cannot resolve. A large youth cohort relative to established adults produces specific pressures - competition for limited formal employment, frustrated status expectation - whatever the governing ideology. (3.9)
acute meaning-collapse: Triage for situations in which meaning infrastructure collapses faster than prospective analysis can address - within days or weeks of sudden regime collapse, forced mass displacement, disinformation saturation, or focal events that destroy the narrative frameworks through which a population organised its experience. The long-run prescriptions for building alternative meaning infrastructure do not operate at this timescale. (5.6d)
power concentration: The claim that concentrating power in a single dominant actor produces systematically dangerous conditions regardless of that actor's ideological commitments. It is an argument from the structure of power, not from sympathy for any counter-hegemonic position, and it applies symmetrically - including against concentration by actors whose stated values align with this framework's own direction. The appropriate check is not a rival concentration but institutional arrangements that make concentration structurally difficult whoever attempts it. (9.2)
conditional normative framework: The status of the framework's normative claims: conditional, not derived. It does not assert that biological facts by themselves entail what ought to be. What follows is conditional - given an arrangement meant to persist and to be inhabited by organisms of this kind, certain conditions must hold. The clarification comes before the biological analysis rather than after it, because the objection it answers would otherwise apply to everything built on top. (3.0)
the naturalistic fallacy objection: The objection that the framework defines normative properties through natural ones - Moore's error of treating the good as equivalent to some natural fact such as the pleasurable or the biologically functional - combined with Hume's related point that descriptive statements do not by themselves entail prescriptive ones. The framework addresses both rather than dismissing either, because its answer determines whether a biological starting point can carry evaluative weight at all. (3.0b)
the teleology reading: The objection that 'becoming' and 'anti-foreclosure' commit the framework to a teleological view of history - development moving toward a terminal state, progress measured by proximity to a fixed destination. It gains surface plausibility from the vocabulary, and is reinforced by the treatment of the last man (4.5) as a failure mode, which implies that some trajectories are worse than others. The framework rejects the reading. (3.0e)
the displacement that matters: What this framework adds to the materialist tradition: the biological floor, the threshold of material conditions below which organisms cannot sustain the cooperation, trust, and institutional engagement that collective life requires. It does not replace the analysis of economic and social conditions; it asks what those conditions are ultimately constrained by - and locates the answer not in the logic of capital nor in the movement of the World Spirit, but in the biology of organisms that can suffer. (3.1)
a typology of suffering: The distinctions the minimal anchor requires, because the criterion applies differently depending on which kind of suffering is at issue: chosen versus imposed, functional versus disfunctional, structural versus incidental, material versus existential. An ascetic tradition that embraces suffering as a path to development is doing something categorically different from an arrangement that imposes deprivation on populations without their meaningful consent. (3.4b)
the maqasid al-shariah: An independent derivation of a structurally equivalent evaluative architecture - a floor of necessary conditions below which no arrangement is legitimate, and a horizon of adaptive response capacity beyond that floor - developed in the Islamic jurisprudential tradition by Al-Ghazali in the twelfth century and systematised by Izz ibn Abd al-Salam in the thirteenth. The parallel is not merely intellectual history: convergence reached from independent foundations is evidence about the structure rather than a borrowing from it. (4.1b)
divine mandate: The objection that the evaluative anchor should be divine command rather than biological suffering. It fails at the level of application before it reaches theology: divine mandates as actually held and practised are incompatible across traditions, so adopting one as the anchor requires a prior selection among them that the mandate itself cannot supply. (4.1c)
rational micro, problematic macro: Individually rational behaviour producing collectively irrational outcomes. Marx saw it in production - each capitalist maximising profit contributes to overproduction, falling rates of profit, and periodic crises that are bad for capitalism as a system. The pattern is not confined to markets: it appears wherever the incentive structure facing individuals diverges from the consequences their aggregate behaviour produces. (3.12)
strategic communication: Communication that accounts for the actual conditions under which people receive information, as distinct from manipulation. The line between them is structural, not a matter of degree or intent: communication that preserves the recipient's capacity to evaluate what is being said is strategic; communication that works by bypassing evaluation is manipulation regardless of whether the content is true. Ignoring the distinction is not principled - it lets correct analysis be defeated by inferior analysis packaged better. (1.6)
the source level and the interface level: The distinction that keeps the metaphysical question open without resolving it prematurely. The source level is whatever exists most fundamentally, operating without preference or intention; the interface level is what appears when consciousness interacts with it, and can be personal and morally engaged whether or not the source level is. The materialist tradition collapsed the distinction in one direction, theistic traditions in the other; both moves exceed the available evidence. (5.2)
the military as autonomous institutional: The military analysed as an institution with its own incentive architecture and capture dynamics rather than as the executive's coercive instrument. The instrumental treatment holds only where civilian control is institutionally robust; it is inadequate for most post-colonial states, for transitional regimes, and increasingly for consolidated democracies - which is to say, for most of the world's population. Its monopoly on organised violence creates leverage asymmetries replicated nowhere else in the institutional landscape. (7.1b)
the long-term direction: Arrangements more globally coordinated, less driven by the competition of territorially bounded states, and more directly accountable to human material welfare across current boundaries. A horizon in the technical sense: an actual horizon recedes as you approach it. Moving toward one is purposive; expecting to stand at one is a category error. The direction is real and its status as an unreachable limit is also real, and not a defect. (7.4)
adaptation, not optimization: Complex adaptive systems do not optimise; they adapt. Optimisation implies a defined target and a metric of progress toward it. Adaptation implies ongoing adjustment without a predetermined endpoint and without a guarantee that adjustment improves anything by a standard external to the system's own survival. Optimisation thinking produces brittle designs that fail when assumed conditions change; adaptation thinking trades efficiency for the capacity to adjust. (10.4)
the sequencing problem: The most important practical problem in political change: identifying the moment at which incremental adjustment is still possible and acting inside that window, rather than accommodating an arrangement past the point where accommodation can work or triggering reorganisation before the conditions for it are in place. It reframes the reform-revolution debate as a question of timing and threshold management rather than of normative preference. (10.6)
micro-politics: The domain in which most political and social life actually occurs - solidarities within neighbourhoods, care networks, mutual aid in workplaces, the daily practices through which structural conditions are reproduced or incrementally subverted. Named as a structural bias the framework must acknowledge: threshold analysis, capture sequences, and agent typology all operate at the macro level. The standard objection that micro-political practice becomes accommodation assumes a zero-sum competition with structural transformation that the record of durable transformations does not support. (10.15)
the seven diagnostic questions: The questions any serious economic analysis must answer, at the framework level, independent of which arrangement is under evaluation. They are the reason the framework produces no blueprint: a framework that generates blueprints has confused its level of operation, treating the diagnostic method as if it were the conclusion the method is supposed to derive. Critics who read the questions as a covert commitment to one arrangement, and defenders who read current doctrine as implied by the framework, make the same error in opposite directions. (11.0)
regulatory capture: The process by which regulatory institutions come to serve the entities they were designed to regulate rather than the populations they were designed to protect. A structural consequence of incentive architecture (7.3c) rather than a product of individual misconduct: the regulated hold concentrated material interests in the institution's decisions, while the protected hold diffuse ones - an asymmetry that operates whatever the character of the officials involved. (11.0b)
framework and doctrine: The two levels the project operates on. The framework is the methodology and aspires to durability; the doctrine is its current application, conditional on present material circumstances and expected to require revision as those change. Capital was not the Communist Manifesto: the Manifesto was doctrine addressed to a specific moment, Capital was the framework given its most rigorous expression. Collapsing the two is the most reliable source of confusion about what the framework commits anyone to. (12.3)
boundary violation detection: The procedure for catching an actor who invokes framework neutrality when criticised while using doctrinal conclusions to direct decisions. The framework-doctrine distinction (12.3) is conceptually clear but operationally fragile - registers can be switched without detection. The tests apply to any claim presented as framework output and do not require the actor to acknowledge the switch: whether the claim follows necessarily from the diagnostic questions, and whether it is structured so that only confirming evidence counts. (12.3b)
the multi-level consequence procedure: The minimum analytical obligation for evaluating any proposed institutional change. First-order analysis - does the arrangement reduce structural suffering and protect adaptive response capacity - is necessary but insufficient. Many arrangements that produce net first-order reductions simultaneously generate second-order conditions producing larger suffering later or for a different population, so analysis that stops at the first order will systematically recommend interventions that improve visible metrics while worsening what determines long-run outcomes. (12.1b)
assumption archaeology: The use of deliberately extreme scenarios - configurations that are not realistic predictions and are not intended to be - to surface assumptions embedded in the framework that stay invisible under realistic cases. It complements stress-testing (12.1) rather than replacing it: stress-testing checks whether structural claims hold under the conditions they were developed for, while extreme scenarios push variables to limits realistic cases never reach, where hidden assumptions become visible structurally. (12.1c)
defeasible inference: The reasoning type the framework consistently employs without naming. Standard propositional logic works with claims that are true or false and inference rules that are truth-preserving; the framework's structural claims do not have that form. They hold under specified conditions and can be defeated by further information without being false. Naming the type matters because it settles what would count as a valid objection - and why formalising the arguments in predicate logic would misrepresent their structure. (12.1d)
essentialist foreclosure: The failure mode of claims about what something is 'essentially' - or at its core, by its nature, fundamentally. The phrase is not always illegitimate, but its characteristic failure is structural: it closes the analytical question that would have been most productive, substituting an assertion about intrinsic nature for an account of the conditions producing the observed behaviour. Paired with 'should' as a diagnostic signal worth treating in its own right. (12.5b)
non-bypassable diagnostic triggers: Four triggers that activate independently of user intent, because identifying failure modes (12.5) is insufficient resistance to misuse: it depends on the analyst recognising their own failure. Misuse by actors who believe they are applying the framework correctly - or who select its vocabulary to legitimise predetermined conclusions - will not be caught by self-monitoring. Satisfying the triggers requires resolving structural contradictions, not making good-faith declarations. (12.5d)
deficit estimation protocol: How analysis proceeds when data is partial, missing, or actively suppressed, without sacrificing the standards that distinguish structural analysis from advocacy. The problem is not incidental: structural suffering is highest where data infrastructure is weakest, so the populations whose conditions most require analysis are often precisely those least documented. A framework that can only operate under adequate data is systematically unavailable where it is most needed. (12.5e)
anti-closure: The conditions under which the appropriate response is replacement rather than revision. Frameworks can simulate openness while never revising at the level of foundational assumptions: internal iteration - adding sections, refining diagnostics, acknowledging gaps - can continue indefinitely without touching the axioms that generate the characteristic outputs. Distinguishing iterative refinement from paradigm-level revision therefore requires external triggers that cannot be internally redefined as already-addressed. (14.4b)
framework institutionalization: The process by which a framework becomes capable of self-correction and survival without depending on any specific individual or community for its integrity. A framework that cannot reproduce itself without distortion across actors, contexts, and time is not a framework - it is a text. Transmission runs through two mechanisms at once, one of which is the compressed core (15.15); transmission by the compressed core is the appropriate form, not a degraded one. (14.5)
self-capture: The application of the capture sequence (7.3b) to a community of practice formed around the framework itself. Not a hypothetical risk: every analytical framework that achieved significant reach generated practitioners with institutional interests in it, and those interests follow the same structural dynamic as any other concentrated interest facing a diffuse one. The framework's own commitments require it to be assessed on this axis rather than exempted from it. (14.6)
accumulated pressure (A): A = S x D x P x G. Duration multiplies suffering's political weight: populations absorb acute crises more readily than chronic conditions, because acute crises do not degrade the behavioural dispositions, life expectations, and institutional trust that chronic suffering erodes. Scale is the proportion of a relevant population affected - below certain thresholds suffering is managed as a minority problem, above them the political arithmetic changes fundamentally. (15.4)
transformation window (Tw): Tw = Cycle Convergence (Cc) x Focal Event Probability (Fe) x Counter-Power Readiness (Cr). The formulas describe structural relationships between variables but are incomplete without a theory of timing: material variables change on several timescales at once - demographic, economic, legitimacy, geopolitical - each on its own tempo, and their intersections create windows of heightened transformation probability. Cycle convergence is not binary but a range. (15.11)
shadow institutions: The organisational forms through which counter-power builds capacity before the conditions for formal institutional seizure exist. The standard answer - that movements build capacity by contesting formal institutions directly - is structurally incomplete, because formal contestation requires resources, legal standing, and public visibility that are typically absent precisely when counter-power is weakest and its need for organisational development is greatest. (10.8b)
the commodification problem: The structural implications of bringing biological processes previously outside market logic within it - in vitro fertilisation, gamete sale and donation, commercial surrogacy, embryo storage and selection. Analytically distinct from the biotechnology analysis of the biological floor (16.3): the issue is not capacity modification but marketisation, with consequences for women who provide reproductive labour, for offspring whose genetic origins are marketised, and for the meaning infrastructure surrounding kinship and bodily integrity. (16.5)
effective accelerationism: The position that the right response to the acceleration dynamic is to accelerate further and faster, trusting that the resulting technical capability will eventually make the present disruption worthwhile. Treated directly rather than dismissed because it is analytically coherent enough to demand engagement and is the operative assumption behind the deployment philosophy of several of the largest technology organisations. Its cost falls on a generation that does not consent to bearing it. (16.4b)
secular rationalism: A family of positions sharing a methodological commitment to reason and empirical evidence as the primary arbiters of belief, but differing substantially on what follows from that commitment at the metaphysical level. The framework inherits the methodological core and explicitly rejects several conclusions that mainstream secular rationalist discourse treats as implications of it - so the question of whether the framework is a form of it and whether it should be are different questions. (2.6)
the projecting fallacy: Applying a category of thought formed within one domain of experience, and valid there, to a domain where it does not apply - then treating the resulting confusion as a refutation of the target rather than a limitation of the tool. The paradigm case is 'who created God?', which imports efficient causation into the question of necessary being and treats the infinite regress it generates as evidence against necessary being, when necessary being is defined as existing without a prior cause. (2.6b)
the supra-rational challenge: The sharpest challenge from religious and post-secular traditions: not whether the material analysis is correct, but whether the criterion has any authority at all. By choosing to evaluate arrangements by their consequences for suffering and becoming, the framework has already decided that suffering and becoming are what matter - and a supra-rational tradition can deny exactly that, without contradicting itself on its own terms. (2.6e)
the stability argument: A second line of response to the naturalistic fallacy objection, frequently misread as a version of it. Arrangements producing mass structural suffering generate observable systemic instability - legitimacy deficits, transformation pressure, institutional breakdown - as measurable causal fact, independent of any commitment about whether that suffering is bad. It does not say that because organisms seek stability it is good for them to have it; it is a predictive claim about causal dynamics, not a normative derivation. (3.0c)
materialist and symbolic approaches: Two routes to the same stated goal that produce genuinely different analyses and different prescriptions. Structural exclusion from resources, opportunity, and institutional protection is what the minimal anchor requires addressing - not because of identity politics, but because exclusion produces unnecessary suffering and the anchor is not selective about which arrangement generates it.
