Analysis begins from what is happening to people and what is producing it, not from the political valence of the group experiencing it. (8.2)
hegemony: Gramsci's name for how a ruling class continues to rule in complex societies where overt coercion is insufficient: the worldview, values, and interpretive frameworks of the dominant class come to be experienced as universal common sense. It names a real mechanism and marks a qualitative advance over orthodox Marxism, which explained why a ruling class rules - control of the means of production - but left underspecified how it keeps ruling once the dominated have organisational capacity and ideological contestation is genuine terrain. (10.7c)
durable positions: Roles in a political ecosystem defined by structural function rather than by individual intent, each with its own characteristic vulnerability. The anchor maintains organisational continuity between moments of heightened activity and is often invisible precisely because the work shows most in its absence; the translator moves between social worlds, making each legible to the other. Positions, not personalities: the same person can occupy different ones at different moments. (10.10c-i)
transitional actors: Actors whose engagement is intense but bounded - mobilised by crises and focal events, contributing counter-power capacity during the period of mobilisation, then returning to positions largely outside the ecosystem. A structural resource that sustained movements must be designed to engage without becoming dependent on: organisational infrastructure that functions only while spontaneous mobilisation is present has failed to build durable capacity. (10.10c-iii)
financialization: The growth in the share of economic activity organised around the creation, trading, and management of financial instruments rather than the production of goods and services. It changes how the seven diagnostic questions (11.0) operate in practice rather than replacing them - which is why taking contemporary capitalism as the terrain for analysis is an identification of the parameters doctrine must work within, not an endorsement of it. (11.3b)
external criticism: Criticism from positions that do not share the framework's starting points and may characterise it in terms it would not use for itself. Not less valid than internal criticism - the genealogical analysis (12.7) establishes that a framework's most consequential blind spots are not visible from inside it. The difficulty is that external criticisms differ in what they actually claim, and applying the wrong response type is itself a failure of engagement. (12.5c)
performative humility: Acknowledging the conditions that produced a framework without letting the acknowledgement change anything about it. The named risk in turning genealogical interrogation (12.6) on the framework itself: applying the method to other claims is incomplete if it is not applied here with equal force, but an honest account of the conditions of production, the interests its acceptance might serve, and the blind spots that follow structurally is not the same as a ritual disclaimer. (12.7)
extreme urgency: The operational condition under which the full five-step assessment procedure (13.4h) must be replaced by triage. Requiring the full procedure in a genuine emergency would itself constitute a moral-functional failure: the time spent on analysis would convert an addressable harm into an irreversible one. It is defined by two conditions holding at once, beginning with credible evidence of severe harm occurring or imminent. (13.4i)
revolutionary capture: Movements that successfully displace existing power arrangements and then reconstruct equivalent structural conditions under new organisational forms. Consistent enough across France 1789-1799, Russia 1917-1928, China 1949-1966, and Iran 1979 to constitute a structural regularity rather than a sequence of individual failures - and not, in the primary instance, cases of ideological corruption or leadership betrayal. It is the custodian problem (7.3) operating at the highest stakes available. (17.4)
platform governance: The question the protection-versus-restriction binary structurally excludes: not whether speech should be protected or restricted, but who controls the institutional architecture through which claims circulate. That architecture determines which claims reach audiences capable of acting on them, at what velocity, amplified by what mechanisms, and open to what contestation. The binary treats the infrastructure as neutral and asks only what content it should carry. (17.5)
drift detection: The shift from diagnostic to practice at the individual scale. The available instruments - the reasoning structure check, the three external signals - are reactive: they identify drift that has already occurred, and a reactive instrument applied after drift is visible is applied too late. Drift is most detectable and most reversible early, before it has been absorbed into the actor's self-understanding as a series of reasonable accommodations, so what matters is a practice built into ordinary activity. (17.7c-ii)
necessary being: The possibility of something whose non-existence is genuinely impossible. The framework is agnostic on it and holds the question open rather than answering it in advance by commitment to material explanation. The observation that raises it is logical, not theological: everything observable is contingent - it could in principle not exist - and that is not settled by the material explanation of any particular thing. From the openness, nothing follows about what such a something would be like. (2.3)
hard materialism: Eliminative materialism: the claim that mental states and subjective experience are nothing but physical processes, and that the apparent irreducibility of experience is an artifact of our current conceptual framework rather than evidence of anything non-physical. Not dismissed - it correctly identifies the causal problems facing dualist accounts, correctly locates experience in the brain, and correctly resists postulating entities beyond what explanation requires. The divergence is over what the third-person domain entitles it to say about the first-person one. (2.6c)
jurisdictional mismatch: Platform infrastructure operating across national jurisdictions simultaneously while regulatory authority remains national. Not an administrative inconvenience but a structural feature of how AI-based platforms accumulate power - by operating at a scale and across boundaries no single regulatory body can address - and in several cases a material advantage deliberately maintained. The custodian problem (7.3) applies here with additional force. (9.2c)
conditional tensions: Tensions that arise from specific conditions - adversarial political contexts, asymmetric information environments, contested public space - rather than from the structure of what human beings are and what collective life requires. Genuine where those conditions exist, but not permanent features of human social existence, and they diminish as the conditions improve. The distinction matters because treating a conditional tension as permanent converts a solvable problem into an accepted one. (13.2b)
the scale of the individual: Where the framework must also be applied if it is to be used honestly. The claim that micro-level decisions are co-constitutive of structural outcomes is not only analytical - it says something about where the analysis has to reach. A framework that analyses institutional capture but cannot help a person detect their own drift is not doing what it claims. What follows is not a code of conduct: it produces questions the holder must be able to answer, including when the answers are inconvenient. (17.7)
weaponized stoicism: Directing a population experiencing structural suffering toward managing their response to it, rather than toward the arrangements producing it. The mechanism is V - visibility suppression (15.0b). The Stoic claim itself is not false, and as a framework for existential suffering, which arises from permanent conditions rather than from arrangements that could be otherwise, the practice has genuine value. The failure is jurisdictional: applying it where structural analysis identifies suffering as unnecessary and changeable. (17.7f)
the transmission problem: A framework that cannot account for its own transmission has analysed how ideas function as material variables everywhere except in its own case. Transmission is not publication: a document that exists and is accessible is not thereby transmitted. It requires reaching people whose material conditions make the tools useful, in a form legible given their existing vocabulary, in an encounter that makes the framework generative rather than merely read. Partly a translation problem - accessible without losing the structural specificity that makes it useful. (17.8)
pancasila and gotong royong: An empirical case in the coalition-across-difference problem (8.6): how to build a political community that holds genuinely different religious, cultural, and ideological commitments together without suppressing any into false uniformity or forcing a choice between them. Pancasila is the five principles Sukarno articulated as the philosophical foundation of the Indonesian Republic, designed to be acceptable to Muslim majority, Christian minority, Hindu Balinese, secular nationalist, and communist constituencies at once; gotong royong is mutual cooperation as an economic and social principle drawn from village practice. The analytical interest is the structural design challenge they address, not the specific content of the principles. (7.2b)
